title: Lengdon and the Nimi Jātaka

claims.label: Source observation
claims.title: Locate Bithila and Mungthila separately
claims.text: Printed page 4 contains the two relevant contexts: §10 for Mungthila and §13 for Bithila. The source locations are checked. A new full Ahom reading is still pending, and the two passages concern different named figures.
claims.locator: Ahom-Buranji, printed p. 4, §§10 and 13 · scan page 10
claims.review: Page location checked, 23 October 2026. Name interpretation also draws on the project dossier of 10 October.

claims.label: Source observation
claims.title: The shared-throne passage is identifiable
claims.text: The passage to collate is printed page 7, §5. The historical English column describes Lengdon and Thenkham sharing a throne and consulting over government. The Ahom crop is provided so an independent reading can be checked against it.
claims.review: The source crop is checked. The historical English description is not relabelled as a fresh translation.

claims.label: Comparative evidence
claims.title: Nimi supplies a relevant royal-heaven narrative
claims.text: Jātaka 541 places Nimi at Mithilā and sends Mātali to bring him to Sakka. The journey includes moral instruction through a tour of hells and heavens. This gives a concrete narrative to compare, while the distinct purposes of the stories must remain visible.
claims.locator: Nimi Jātaka 541; the invitation and journey sections
claims.review: English primary-text translation consulted for this release. Comparison is not a claim of direct textual dependence.

claims.label: Comparative evidence
claims.title: The motif does not identify Nimi uniquely
claims.text: The project’s source audit also compares Sādhina Jātaka 494, another Mithilā king’s encounter with Sakka, including shared sovereignty. A shared seat or heavenly host needs to be tested against this wider narrative tradition.
claims.locator: Sādhina Jātaka 494; project audit, 10 October 2026, pp. 4–5
claims.review: Alternative comparison retained to avoid treating a widely shared motif as unique evidence.

claims.label: Manuscript lead
claims.title: An Ahom Nemi witness strengthens the research question
claims.text: The earlier audit identifies Nemi Mang in the EAP catalogue and records alternative copying dates within the Ahom monarchy. A catalogue identification supports a manuscript lead; it does not establish the date of the story’s first arrival or name a royal patron.
claims.review: Inherited catalogue finding. Live verification and a new colophon reading remain pending.

claims.label: Open hypothesis
claims.title: Buddhist adaptation is plausible; the exact route remains open
claims.text: The place-name correspondences, royal-heaven motif and Nemi witness make Buddhist adaptation a serious question. They do not yet demonstrate that the complete Lengdon foundation story derives exclusively from Nimi, or that every Ahom ruler practised Buddhism.
claims.locator: Synthesis from the project’s 10 October 2026 source audit
claims.review: Research inference, not a certified translation or a settled historical conclusion.

status: Inherited project dossier, 23 October 2026; not independently reverified in release 0.2.

studies.status: Summary of the completed 28 October 2026 research synthesis; not an independent verification of every cited witness. Chinese translations are working renderings. The conventional 1215/1228 migration chronology is discussed as contested, not fixed independently.

claims.label: Documented regional evidence
claims.title: Contact and continuity in a connected region
claims.text: The study finds strong textual support for Nanzhao conquest, recruitment and population transfers in western Yunnan and the Upper Ayeyarwady world. Ahom linguistic relationships and the later-transmitted Maolung origin tradition supply a Tai/Shan regional connection. These are different forms of evidence; the records do not identify an Ahom contingent or a continuous royal pedigree.
claims.locator: Report pp. 2–5, 7–9; Chinese historical accounts and the chronology.

claims.label: Plausible historical connections
claims.title: Transmission mechanisms remain hypotheses
claims.text: Military service, relocation, court exchange and circulating texts offer plausible channels for cultural transmission. Particular claims about Ahom institutions, titles or narratives still need dated intermediate witnesses. Shared geography and similar names or motifs do not by themselves establish a route of borrowing.
claims.locator: Report pp. 2–3, 7–9; source-critical method and contact mechanisms.

claims.label: Unverified genealogy
claims.title: Direct descent from Nanzhao rulers is not established
claims.text: No corroborated genealogy linking Sukaphaa’s house to Nanzhao’s Meng rulers was located in the inspected evidence. Regional continuity is not proof of dynastic descent. The study leaves this interpretation unverified and identifies the need for additional linking evidence.
claims.locator: Report p. 2 and p. 32; principal assessment and research limits.

studies.status: Summary attributed to the original nine-page report of 29 October 2026. The original is preserved unchanged. Its incomplete access to early scholarship is a historical limitation of that report; the separate supplement directly examines Singh’s complete 1980 article. This Atlas integration reads the two reports, not every underlying original.

claims.label: Published object record
claims.title: A recorded coin type with a debated attribution
claims.text: The report uses Spink auction 16041, lot 258 (2016; RB A7.1), for the octagonal silver rupee, its Chinese characters and numeral 1570. The working description is an Ahom-attributed rupee, conventionally Saka 1570 (1648–1649 CE), catalogued under Jayadhvaja Simha. This identifies a published type; it does not independently authenticate the photographed specimen.
claims.locator: Original report pp. 1–2, source [1]; supplement pp. 3, 9 and 11, [S04, S10].

claims.label: Trade interpretation
claims.title: Regional commerce does not settle this coin’s market
claims.text: The report treats Tibetan trade as a prominent published explanation and China through Yunnan as an alternative reported through bibliography. Independent evidence for Assam’s Himalayan commerce supplies context. It does not establish where this rare issue circulated, why it ceased, or any Nanzhao dynastic ancestry. The supplement refines the attribution debate and access record.
claims.locator: Original report pp. 3, 5–7, [2–4, 7–10]; supplement pp. 8 and 11.

studies.status: Summary attributed to the 15-page source-critical supplement of 29 October 2026. Direct and indirect access labels below describe the supplement’s investigation. Reading a complete scholarly article establishes what its author argues; it does not turn that argument into a contemporary mint record or a settled attribution.

claims.label: Attribution debate
claims.title: Jayadhvaja is the catalogue convention; Pratapa is a documented alternative
claims.text: Singh’s complete 1980 article, pp. 245–247, argues for Pratapa Simha through chronology, a chronicle passage and analogy with anonymous Sanskrit issues. Neither ruler’s name is read on the Chinese-character coin. The supplement traces Allan’s 1909 Sanskrit-series attribution and Botham’s 1914 rebuttal; Rhodes (2001) and Spink (2016) retain Jayadhvaja. The convention remains qualified because the decisive chronology and inscription have not been independently collated.
claims.locator: Supplement pp. 4–6 and 11, [S04, S07–S11]. Allan and Botham discuss Sanskrit comparators, not a Chinese-coin findspot.

claims.label: Direct and indirect scholarship
claims.title: One early access gap is resolved; two remain
claims.text: The supplement directly reads Singh (1980), Botham (1914), Rhodes’s 1978 letter and his 2001 article. Rhodes’s 1975 original was located with restricted PDF/OCR and was not read. Chowdhuri and Ray’s complete article and plate were not obtained: Singh supplies an indirect account of their China proposal, while Bertsch’s annotated entry supplies the Yunnan route. Those accounts are not a substitute for the original.
claims.locator: Supplement pp. 2, 8 and 12–15; [S02–S04, S06, S08, S11–S12].

claims.label: Unresolved purposes
claims.title: Tibet, Yunnan and diplomacy remain interpretations
claims.text: Tibetan trade is retained by Rhodes’s later statements and the auction catalogue. China through Yunnan is a published competing lead known indirectly. Singh also proposes distinctive domestic coinage and a possible diplomatic overture seeking Chinese help against the Mughals. The supplement finds no decisive mint order, secure route-specific find or relevant embassy record. These are attributed proposals; their intended market and purpose remain uncertain.
claims.locator: Supplement pp. 8–11; Singh p. 246; [S04, S10–S13]. The evidential assessment is the supplement’s inference.

claims.label: Correction attached to Deyell
claims.title: Keep the existing Deyell reference with its published correction
claims.text: The supplement reads Deyell’s Ahom-language coin study alongside Rhodes’s September 1978 correction (pp. 278–279), published with Deyell’s approval: the supposed Suklenmung issue of 1543 is reassigned to Shupungmung in 1663. This corrects a comparator series and supports careful legend-reading; it does not identify the ruler or destination of the Chinese-character type. The existing Allan and Deyell catalogue records are linked below and remain unchanged.
